title: Home
text:
Pilot episode
In the outset, I am going to make a list of different ways in which neuroscience and the law interact. This is certainly not an exhaustive list, but it helps to preview what’s ahead and begin building a big source from which we can, later in this project, pull into the spotlight and research more deeply:

how neuroscience understands human behavior
regulation of neurotechnologies, like consumer devices that record neural data. Neurorights: the rights of an individual to their neural data, and its privacy.

I anticipate drawing from the Neurorights Foundation at Columbia and elsewhere.

how effective are the current legal, enforcement, and penal systems in molding human behavior?

for instance,

juvenile culpability: are young folks

free will and moral blameworthiness

what does neuroscience tell us about the existence of free will?
let’s assume free will does not exist. How should our legal systems be constructed with this understanding?



Module 1. Learning two languages, and building a lingua franca
A lot of work in neurolaw, I think, is learning the (quite distinct) languages of the fields of neuroscience and the law.

Juvenile culpability

Roper v. Simmons (2005) - banned juvenile execution
Graham v. Florida (2010) - banned life without parole for juveniles in non-homicide cases
Miller v. Alabama (2012) - extended Graham to homicide cases: banned mandatory life without parole for juveniles, even in homicide cases
Montgomery v. Louisiana (2016) - made Miller retroactive, so those sentenced prior to Miller could seek resentencing
